name: WHO: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health
title: WHO: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health
answer: The World Health Organization publishes the reference guidance on ethics and governance of AI for health, the product of eighteen months of expert deliberation and earlier international consultations. It sets out the ethical risks of AI in health, six consensus principles to ensure AI works to the public benefit of all countries, and recommendations holding public and private stakeholders accountable to health workers and the communities affected by these technologies.

sections.body: This is the World Health Organization's guidance on the ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health, published on who.int and announced in a news item dated 28 June 2021. WHO describes it as its first global report on AI in health, produced after two years of consultations by a panel of international experts appointed by WHO. Elsewhere the organisation describes the guidance as the product of eighteen months of deliberation among leading experts in ethics, digital technology, law and human rights, as well as experts from Ministries of Health. The work builds on earlier WHO activity, including a 2017 international consultation with the University of Miami Collaborating Centre, a special symposium at the World Congress of Bioethics in Bangalore in December 2018, and an international consultation held from 2 to 4 October 2019 with participants from government, inter-governmental agencies, academia, civil society and industry.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: WHO states that AI can be, and in some wealthy countries already is being used to improve the speed and accuracy of diagnosis and screening for diseases, to assist with clinical care, to strengthen health research and drug development, and to support public health interventions such as disease surveillance, outbreak response and health systems management. The report cautions against overestimating the benefits of AI for health, especially when this happens at the expense of core investments and strategies required to achieve universal health coverage. It identifies risks including unethical collection and use of health data, biases encoded in algorithms, and risks to patient safety, cybersecurity and the environment. It warns that unregulated use of AI could subordinate the rights and interests of patients and communities to the commercial interests of technology companies or to governments' interests in surveillance and social control, and notes that systems trained primarily on data from high-income countries may not perform well in low- and middle-income settings. The report sets out six consensus principles to ensure AI works to the public benefit of all countries, and a set of recommendations intended to maximise the promise of the technology while holding all stakeholders in the public and private sector accountable and responsive to the healthcare workers who will rely on these technologies and to the communities and individuals whose health will be affected. According to the report, new technologies that use artificial intelligence must put ethics and human rights at the heart of their design, deployment and use.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source gives the six guiding principles as protecting human autonomy, promoting human well-being and safety and the public interest, ensuring transparency, explainability and intelligibility, and fostering responsibility and accountability, with the news item listing these among the six. It states that the guidance followed two years of consultations by a WHO-appointed international expert panel, or eighteen months of deliberation among leading experts, depending on the page. It dates the international consultation to 2 to 4 October 2019, the Bangalore symposium to December 2018, and the earlier WHO and University of Miami consultation to 2017. It also notes that a theme issue of the WHO Bulletin on big data, machine learning and AI was to be published in 2020.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For anyone following AI in healthcare, this is the governance frame that national health systems are expected to work within. It is the document that names the risks regulators and health ministries must address, from biased algorithms and unethical data use to patient safety and cybersecurity, and it supplies the six principles that member states and vendors are likely to be measured against. Its recommendations address both the public and private sector, which makes it useful for understanding how procurement, deployment and accountability for clinical AI are being framed internationally, and its warning about overestimating AI's benefits is a counterweight to vendor claims.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Healthcare

sections.body: The pages read are publication and news pages rather than the full text of the guidance, so they summarise the report's principles, risks and recommendations without reproducing its detailed provisions. The material is dated, with the news item from June 2021 and preparatory consultations from 2017 to 2019, and it does not cover regulatory or technical developments since. It is guidance and ethical framing rather than operational instruction, and the pages give no implementation data, cost figures or country-level results.
